blocks.en: Arm Yourself with the Mind of Christ
blocks.es_reference: Armaos del Mismo Pensamiento de Cristo

blocks.en: Peter has just set Christ before us as the One who suffered, died, and now reigns. Now he draws the practical lesson. "Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind, for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, that he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God" (1 Peter 4:1-2). The word arm is a soldier's word; the believer is to take up the same attitude Christ had as a weapon for the battle ahead. Christ was willing to suffer in the flesh rather than turn aside from the will of God, and the believer is to share that resolve. The one who has so suffered — who has died with Christ to the old way of living — has made a decisive break with sin. As a result, he will no longer spend the rest of his life chasing the lusts of men; he will spend it doing the will of God. The whole direction of life is turned around: from the appetites of the flesh to the will of the Father.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro acaba de poner a Cristo delante de nosotros como Aquel que padeció, murió y ahora reina. Ahora saca la lección práctica. "Pues que Cristo ha padecido por nosotros en la carne, vosotros también armaos del mismo pensamiento; que el que ha padecido en la carne, cesó de pecado; para que ya el tiempo que queda en la carne, viva, no a las concupiscencias de los hombres, sino a la voluntad de Dios" (1 Pedro 4:1-2). La palabra armaos es palabra de soldado; el creyente ha de tomar la misma actitud que tuvo Cristo como un arma para la batalla que viene. Cristo estuvo dispuesto a padecer en la carne antes que apartarse de la voluntad de Dios, y el creyente ha de compartir esa resolución. El que así ha padecido — el que ha muerto con Cristo al viejo modo de vivir — ha hecho una ruptura decisiva con el pecado. Por tanto, ya no gastará el resto de su vida persiguiendo las concupiscencias de los hombres; la gastará haciendo la voluntad de Dios. Toda la dirección de la vida queda vuelta del revés: de los apetitos de la carne a la voluntad del Padre.

blocks.en: Done with the Old Life
blocks.es_reference: Terminado con la Vida Vieja

blocks.en: Peter speaks plainly about the past these believers had left behind. "For we have spent enough of our past lifetime in doing the will of the Gentiles — when we walked in lewdness, lusts, drunkenness, revelries, drinking parties, and abominable idolatries" (1 Peter 4:3). The point is simple and bracing: enough. Whatever time was wasted in the old pagan ways, it was more than enough; there is no reason to give it another hour. But such a clean break does not go unnoticed. "In regard to these, they think it strange that you do not run with them in the same flood of dissipation, speaking evil of you" (1 Peter 4:4). The old companions are baffled and even offended that the believer no longer plunges with them into the same rushing stream of excess, and they repay his changed life with slander. Yet they are not the final judges. "They will give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead" (1 Peter 4:5). Everyone, slanderer and saint alike, must answer to God, who is ready to judge all. It is in this connection that Peter says the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead (1 Peter 4:6) — that is, to believers who heard the good news while they lived and have since died; though they were judged as all men are, dying in the flesh, they live according to God in the spirit. Death is not the end for those who have heard and believed.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro habla claramente del pasado que estos creyentes habían dejado atrás. "Porque nos debe bastar que el tiempo pasado de nuestra vida hayamos hecho la voluntad de los gentiles, andando en lascivias, concupiscencias, embriagueces, glotonerías, orgías de beber, y abominables idolatrías" (1 Pedro 4:3). El punto es sencillo y firme: basta. Cualquier tiempo que se desperdició en las viejas costumbres paganas, fue más que suficiente; no hay razón para darle otra hora. Pero una ruptura tan limpia no pasa inadvertida. "Y esto parece extraño a los que os vituperan, que vosotros no corráis con ellos en el mismo desenfreno de disolución" (1 Pedro 4:4). Los viejos compañeros quedan perplejos y aun ofendidos de que el creyente ya no se lance con ellos al mismo torrente desbordado de exceso, y pagan su vida cambiada con calumnia. Mas ellos no son los jueces finales. "Los cuales darán cuenta al que está preparado para juzgar a los vivos y a los muertos" (1 Pedro 4:5). Todos, calumniador y santo por igual, han de responder a Dios, que está preparado para juzgar a todos. Es en este sentido que Pedro dice que el evangelio fue predicado aun a los que ahora están muertos (1 Pedro 4:6) — es decir, a los creyentes que oyeron las buenas nuevas mientras vivían y han muerto desde entonces; aunque fueron juzgados como todos los hombres, muriendo en la carne, viven según Dios en el espíritu. La muerte no es el fin para los que han oído y creído.

blocks.en: The End Is Near: Sober and Watchful
blocks.es_reference: El Fin Está Cerca: Templados y Velando

blocks.en: "But the end of all things is at hand; therefore be serious and watchful in your prayers." — 1 Peter 4:7 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Mas el fin de todas las cosas se acerca; sed pues templados, y velad en oración." — 1 Pedro 4:7 (RVG)

blocks.en: "But the end of all things is at hand; therefore be serious and watchful in your prayers" (1 Peter 4:7). A fair question arises here, for Peter, Paul, and John all spoke of the end as near, and that was many centuries ago. Were they mistaken? They were not, and two things must be remembered. First, nearness must be measured from God's perspective, not ours. Scripture reminds us that with the Lord a thousand years are as a day, and a day as a thousand years; so from God's vantage point only a short while has passed since Peter wrote. Second, there is a nearness that touches every person directly. Given the uncertainties of life, and knowing that on average we live only some seventy years, the end is truly near for every one of us — our own end may come at any moment. So the warning is not an error to be explained away but a truth to be felt. And the response Peter calls for is practical: be serious, sober-minded, and watchful in prayer. The shortness of the time should sharpen our prayers and steady our minds, not throw us into panic or idleness.
blocks.es_reference: "Mas el fin de todas las cosas se acerca; sed pues templados, y velad en oración" (1 Pedro 4:7). Surge aquí una pregunta justa, pues Pedro, Pablo y Juan hablaron todos del fin como cercano, y eso fue hace muchos siglos. ¿Se equivocaron? No se equivocaron, y dos cosas deben recordarse. Primero, la cercanía debe medirse desde la perspectiva de Dios, no la nuestra. La Escritura nos recuerda que para el Señor mil años son como un día, y un día como mil años; así que desde el punto de vista de Dios solo ha pasado un breve tiempo desde que Pedro escribió. Segundo, hay una cercanía que toca a cada persona directamente. Dadas las incertidumbres de la vida, y sabiendo que en promedio vivimos solo unos setenta años, el fin está verdaderamente cerca para cada uno de nosotros — nuestro propio fin puede llegar en cualquier momento. Así que la advertencia no es un error que explicar sino una verdad que sentir. Y la respuesta que Pedro pide es práctica: sed serios, de mente sobria, y velad en oración. La brevedad del tiempo debe agudizar nuestras oraciones y serenar nuestras mentes, no arrojarnos al pánico ni a la pereza.

blocks.en: Above All, Fervent Love
blocks.es_reference: Sobre Todo, Ferviente Amor

blocks.en: From the call to prayer Peter moves to the supreme Christian duty. "And above all things have fervent love for one another, for 'love will cover a multitude of sins'" (1 Peter 4:8). Notice the priority: above all things. Of all the graces a believer may pursue, love for one another stands first. The word fervent pictures love stretched out to its full reach, love that keeps going when it would be easier to give up. And such love, Peter says, will cover a multitude of sins. This does not mean love ignores wrongdoing or calls evil good; it means that love readily forgives, overlooks small offenses, and refuses to broadcast or brood over the faults of others. In a suffering church, where believers are pressed close together and nerves can wear thin, this fervent, forgiving love is the very bond that holds the family of God together. Where love is fervent, a thousand small grievances are quietly covered and never allowed to divide.
blocks.es_reference: Del llamado a la oración Pedro pasa al deber cristiano supremo. "Y sobre todo, tened entre vosotros ferviente amor; porque el amor cubrirá multitud de pecados" (1 Pedro 4:8). Note la prioridad: sobre todo. De todas las gracias que un creyente pueda buscar, el amor de unos por otros está primero. La palabra ferviente retrata un amor extendido hasta su pleno alcance, un amor que sigue adelante cuando sería más fácil rendirse. Y tal amor, dice Pedro, cubrirá multitud de pecados. Esto no significa que el amor pase por alto el mal hacer ni llame bueno al mal; significa que el amor perdona prontamente, pasa por alto las pequeñas ofensas, y rehúsa pregonar o rumiar las faltas de los demás. En una iglesia que sufre, donde los creyentes están apretados unos contra otros y los nervios pueden gastarse, este amor ferviente y perdonador es el vínculo mismo que mantiene unida a la familia de Dios. Donde el amor es ferviente, mil pequeños agravios quedan calladamente cubiertos y nunca se les permite dividir.

blocks.en: Stewards of the Manifold Grace of God
blocks.es_reference: Administradores de la Multiforme Gracia de Dios

blocks.en: Now Peter comes to the theme that gives this unit its name. "Be hospitable to one another without grumbling. As each one has received a gift, minister it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God" (1 Peter 4:9-10). First comes hospitality — an open home and an open heart — offered cheerfully, without grumbling about the cost or the trouble. Then comes the great principle: every believer has received a gift, and the important word is steward. A steward is a manager. The clearest picture is Joseph, who managed all of Potiphar's household; he owned nothing there, yet everything was entrusted to his care. That is precisely the Christian's position. Everything we are and everything we have is not our own to spend as we please but is entrusted to us to be used in the service of God. It has been observed that nearly half of the parables Jesus told touch on stewardship; again and again He taught that our talents, our time, and our treasures belong to God, and that we are only managers who must one day give account.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora Pedro llega al tema que da nombre a esta unidad. "Hospedaos los unos a los otros sin murmuraciones. Cada uno según el don que ha recibido, minístrelo a los otros, como buenos administradores de la multiforme gracia de Dios" (1 Pedro 4:9-10). Primero viene la hospitalidad — una casa abierta y un corazón abierto — ofrecida con alegría, sin murmurar por el costo o la molestia. Luego viene el gran principio: cada creyente ha recibido un don, y la palabra importante es administrador. Un administrador es un gerente. El retrato más claro es José, que administraba toda la casa de Potifar; nada le pertenecía allí, y sin embargo todo estaba confiado a su cuidado. Esa es precisamente la posición del cristiano. Todo lo que somos y todo lo que tenemos no es nuestro para gastarlo a nuestro gusto, sino que nos está confiado para usarlo en el servicio de Dios. Se ha observado que casi la mitad de las parábolas que Jesús contó tocan la administración; una y otra vez enseñó que nuestros talentos, nuestro tiempo y nuestros tesoros pertenecen a Dios, y que solo somos gerentes que un día darán cuenta.

blocks.en: A striking example is C. T. Studd, once the finest cricket player in all of England. When he became a Christian he gave himself to the mission field, and when a large inheritance came to him from his father, he gave it all away to the work of the gospel. Near the end of his life he was dismayed to discover that some money still remained in his hands, and he quickly passed it on to General Booth of the Salvation Army; he was determined not to leave this world holding any monetary wealth of his own. Few are called to do exactly as he did, but his spirit is the spirit of a true steward, who holds even great wealth with an open hand, counting it God's and not his own.
blocks.es_reference: Un ejemplo notable es C. T. Studd, en otro tiempo el mejor jugador de críquet de toda Inglaterra. Cuando llegó a ser cristiano se entregó al campo misionero, y cuando le vino una gran herencia de su padre, la regáló toda a la obra del evangelio. Cerca del fin de su vida quedó consternado al descubrir que aún le quedaba algo de dinero en las manos, y rápidamente se lo pasó al general Booth del Ejército de Salvación; estaba resuelto a no dejar este mundo reteniendo riqueza monetaria propia. Pocos son llamados a hacer exactamente lo que él hizo, pero su espíritu es el espíritu de un verdadero administrador, que sostiene aun la gran riqueza con mano abierta, contándola de Dios y no suya.

blocks.en: It is worth pausing on the word each. Peter says that each one has received a gift; not a few gifted leaders only, but every single believer. There is no such thing as a Christian with nothing to contribute, and no such thing as a Christian who may sit idle while others serve. The grace of God is called manifold, that is, many-colored and varied, because God distributes a wonderful variety of gifts throughout His people, and each gift is needed. The quiet servant and the gifted teacher, the one who shows mercy and the one who gives, the encourager and the helper — all are stewards entrusted with a portion of God’s grace for the good of the whole body. To bury one’s gift, or to despise it as too small, is to fail as a steward; the Master gave it to be used.
blocks.es_reference: Vale la pena detenerse en la palabra cada. Pedro dice que cada uno ha recibido un don; no unos pocos líderes dotados solamente, sino cada creyente. No existe tal cosa como un cristiano que no tenga nada que aportar, ni tal cosa como un cristiano que pueda quedarse ocioso mientras otros sirven. La gracia de Dios se llama multiforme, es decir, de muchos colores y variada, porque Dios reparte una maravillosa variedad de dones por todo su pueblo, y cada don es necesario. El siervo callado y el maestro dotado, el que muestra misericordia y el que da, el que anima y el que ayuda — todos son administradores a quienes se ha confiado una porción de la gracia de Dios para el bien de todo el cuerpo. Enterrar el propio don, o despreciarlo por pequeño, es fallar como administrador; el Señor lo dio para que se usara.

blocks.en: Peter then shows how this stewardship works in the body of Christ. "If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God. If anyone ministers, let him do it as with the ability which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen" (1 Peter 4:11). The believer who teaches or speaks is to handle his words as the very words of God, with reverence and care. The believer who serves in any practical way is to do it by the strength God supplies, not in his own power. And the goal of it all is not the servant's reputation but this: that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. Our gifts are entrusted grace, to be spent for others and for the glory of God.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro muestra entonces cómo obra esta administración en el cuerpo de Cristo. "Si alguno habla, hable conforme a los oráculos de Dios; si alguno ministra, ministre conforme al poder que Dios da; para que en todo sea Dios glorificado por Jesucristo, a quien es gloria e imperio por los siglos de los siglos. Amén" (1 Pedro 4:11). El creyente que enseña o habla ha de tratar sus palabras como las palabras mismas de Dios, con reverencia y cuidado. El creyente que sirve de cualquier manera práctica ha de hacerlo por la fuerza que Dios da, no en su propio poder. Y la meta de todo ello no es la reputación del siervo sino esta: que en todo sea Dios glorificado por Jesucristo. Nuestros dones son gracia confiada, para gastarse por los demás y para la gloria de Dios.

blocks.en: "...that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen." — 1 Peter 4:11 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...para que en todo sea Dios glorificado por Jesucristo, a quien es gloria e imperio por los siglos de los siglos. Amén." — 1 Pedro 4:11 (RVG)

sa.prompt: Explain verses 1-2 — arming yourself with the mind of Christ and living for the will of God.
sa.model: Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, the believer is to arm himself with the same mind, taking up Christ's attitude as a weapon for the battle ahead. Christ was willing to suffer rather than turn from the will of God, and the believer is to share that resolve. The one who has so suffered, who has died with Christ to the old way of living, has ceased from sin, having made a decisive break with it. As a result, he no longer lives the rest of his time in the flesh for the lusts of men but for the will of God. The whole direction of his life is turned around, away from the appetites of the flesh and toward the will of the Father, so that suffering itself becomes a mark of being done with sin and given over to God.

sa.prompt: Explain verses 3-4 — the break with the old life and the reaction of former companions.
sa.model: Peter says believers have spent enough of their past lifetime doing the will of the Gentiles, walking in lewdness, lusts, drunkenness, revelry, and idolatry; whatever time was wasted in the old pagan life, it was more than enough, and there is no reason to give it another hour. But so clean a break does not go unnoticed. The old companions think it strange that the believer no longer runs with them in the same flood of dissipation, and they repay his changed life by speaking evil of him and slandering him. Yet they are not the final judges, for they will give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. The believer must let the break with the past stand firm, even when the old crowd is baffled and turns hostile.

sa.prompt: Explain verses 5-6 — accountability to the Judge of the living and the dead.
sa.model: Peter warns that those who slander the believers will give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead; no one escapes that reckoning, and God will set every wrong right. It is in this connection that Peter says the gospel was preached also to those who are now dead. This is best understood of believers who heard the good news while they were alive and have since died. Though they were judged as all men are judged, dying in the flesh, they live according to God in the spirit. So the death of believers is not defeat; having heard and believed the gospel, they pass through the common human judgment of death yet live on with God. The certainty of a final reckoning, and of life beyond death for the faithful, steadies the believer who is slandered now.

sa.prompt: Explain Peter's treatment of verse 7 — in what sense is 'the end of all things at hand'?
sa.model: A fair question arises, since Peter, Paul, and John all spoke of the end as near, and that was many centuries ago. Were they mistaken? They were not, and two things must be remembered. First, nearness must be measured from God's perspective, not ours; Scripture reminds us that with the Lord a thousand years are as a day and a day as a thousand years, so from God's vantage point only a short while has passed since Peter wrote. Second, there is a nearness that touches every person directly. Given the uncertainties of life, and knowing that on average we live only about seventy years, the end is truly near for every one of us, since our own end may come at any moment. So the nearness of the end is not an error to be explained away but a sober truth, and it calls the believer to be watchful and ready.

sa.prompt: Explain verse 8 and the supremacy of love in the Christian life.
sa.model: Peter places fervent love for one another above all things; of all the graces a believer may pursue, love stands supreme and first. The word fervent pictures love stretched out to its full reach, love that keeps going when it would be easier to give up. Such love, Peter says, will cover a multitude of sins. This does not mean love ignores wrongdoing or calls evil good; it means love readily forgives, overlooks small offenses, and refuses to broadcast or brood over the faults of others. In a suffering church, where believers are pressed close together and nerves can wear thin, this fervent, forgiving love is the bond that holds the family of God together. Where love is fervent, a multitude of small grievances are quietly covered and never allowed to divide the people of God, so love is to be the believer's first and supreme pursuit.

sa.prompt: Explain the meaning of 'steward' in verse 10, using the lesson's examples.
sa.model: The key word in verse 10 is steward, which means a manager. The clearest picture is Joseph, who managed all of Potiphar's household; he owned nothing there, yet everything was entrusted to his care. That is precisely the Christian's position before God. Everything we are and everything we have is not our own to spend as we please but is entrusted to us to be used in the service of God. It has been observed that nearly half of the parables Jesus told touch on stewardship, for again and again He taught that our talents, our time, and our treasures all belong to God, and that we are only managers of what He has placed in our hands. As stewards, we will one day give account for how faithfully we have managed the Master's gifts, and so we are to use all that we have, not for ourselves, but for Him.

sa.prompt: Explain the example of C.T. Studd and what it teaches about stewardship.
sa.model: C. T. Studd, once the finest cricket player in all of England, became a Christian and gave himself to the mission field. When a large inheritance came to him from his father, he gave it all away to the work of the gospel. Near the end of his life he was dismayed to discover that some money still remained in his hands, and he quickly passed it on to General Booth of the Salvation Army, determined not to leave this world holding any monetary wealth of his own. His example teaches radical stewardship. He treated his money as God's and not his own, and refused to cling to it for himself. Few are called to do exactly as he did, but his spirit is the spirit of a true steward, who holds even great wealth with an open hand, ready to spend it all in the service of God rather than hoard it.

sa.prompt: Explain verses 9-11 — how believers are to use their gifts as stewards of God's grace.
sa.model: Peter says be hospitable to one another without grumbling, offering an open home and heart cheerfully. Then he gives the great principle: as each one has received a gift, he is to minister it to one another as a good steward of the manifold grace of God. Every believer has received some gift, and it is given not for himself but to serve others; he is to use it as a manager of God's varied grace. Peter then shows how this works in the body. The one who speaks is to speak as the very oracles of God, with reverence and care. The one who serves is to do it by the strength that God supplies, not in his own power. And the goal of it all is not the servant's reputation but that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. Our gifts are entrusted grace, to be spent for others and for the glory of God.

sa.prompt: How do verses 7-11 connect the nearness of the end with the believer's duties of prayer, love, and service?
sa.model: Because the end of all things is at hand, Peter draws out practical duties rather than idle speculation. First, the believer is to be serious, sober-minded, and watchful in prayer, living alertly because the time is short. Second, above all he is to keep fervent love for one another, the love that covers a multitude of sins. Third, he is to show hospitality without grumbling and to minister whatever gift he has received as a good steward of God's manifold grace, serving by the strength God supplies. So the nearness of the end is not an excuse for panic or laziness but a powerful motive for prayer, love, and faithful service. The shortness of the time sharpens the believer's devotion to God and to others, and the aim through it all is that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.

sa.prompt: Summarize the central message of Unit 10 (1 Peter 4:1-11).
sa.model: Unit 10 teaches the believer how to live in the short time that remains. Since Christ suffered in the flesh, believers arm themselves with His mind and, having broken with sin, live the rest of their lives for the will of God rather than the old pagan ways, even when former companions slander them. Those slanderers will answer to the Judge of the living and the dead. Because the end of all things is at hand, near both from God's perspective and for each of us personally, believers are to be sober and watchful in prayer, and above all to keep fervent love, which covers a multitude of sins. And as each one has received a gift, he is to minister it as a good steward of the manifold grace of God, speaking as God's oracles and serving by God's strength, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.
